storylines.label: Deep Research
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Shandu 4.0 – Local sleek deep research agent that audits every citation

editorial.tldr: This is a research-theme thread, not one event: through October and early November, papers reworked deep research agents around iterative state, video sources and page-image input. On Nov 12 and Nov 25 the focus moved to multi-agent coordination and to scoring report coverage.
editorial.whats_new: On Nov 27, Shandu 4.0 shipped as an open-source local deep research agent that checks every cited sentence against its source text, with any LiteLLM-supported model.
editorial.why_it_matters: Deep research is moving from demos to measurable systems: coordination cost, rubric-scored coverage and per-sentence citation checks are now concrete things to evaluate in your own research agent.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you ship a research agent, add a per-sentence citation check against retrieved source text before release, and score report coverage with rubrics instead of judging fluency.

status.detail: Loosely linked work on how deep research agents split work, get scored and prove their citations.

storylines.label: Knowledge Engineering
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Dev-Mem – Local-first SQLite knowledge graph for AI coding agents

editorial.tldr: This thread has been narrowed from a 77-item "large language" bucket to 8 items about knowledge engineering: LLM agents that build taxonomies, ontologies and knowledge graphs. It is a research theme, not one event: arXiv papers on agent-built knowledge bases ran alongside Netflix's Nov 13 production knowledge graph for observability agents.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 26: Dev-Mem, a Show HN tool, gives Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and OpenCode a local SQLite store of past decisions, failed approaches and constraints, injected into each new session and optionally shared via Git.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent context is moving from retrieved chunks to curated, structured knowledge (ontologies, graphs, decision logs), so platform teams now own a knowledge base that needs schema, freshness and review like any other data store.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you give coding agents a persistent memory store such as Dev-Mem, review entries like code: it is injected into every session, so a stale "failed approach" or wrong constraint will steer each future run until someone deletes it.

storylines.label: Nemotron 3.5
storylines.latest_title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

editorial.tldr: Nemotron 3.5 launched in October with day-0 vLLM support for Super VL, added speech with Transcribe, and picked up an AWS EKS guide by Oct 29. In November AWS put Super VL into SageMaker JumpStart, and two arXiv papers followed: a 4GB small model for conversational agents and an RL post-training study on Super.
editorial.whats_new: NVIDIA released three synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe and a DFlash speculator for faster inference for Nemotron 3.5 Parse, its document-parsing model, on Nov 26.
editorial.why_it_matters: Nemotron 3.5 is turning from one hosted model into a family you can fine-tune and serve yourself, from a 4GB agent model to a 120B multimodal model, each with open data or recipes.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you parse PDFs or scans in a RAG pipeline, fine-tune Parse on your own documents with the released recipe and measure the DFlash speculator's latency before swapping out your current parser.

status.detail: Super VL is one-click on SageMaker JumpStart; the family now includes a small agent model and a Parse model with open datasets and a speculator.

storylines.label: Multi-Agent Systems
storylines.latest_title: Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

editorial.tldr: This is a theme thread, not one event: three weeks of mostly arXiv work on what breaks when LLM agents run as a team, starting with WorkflowArena's benchmark for harnesses that spawn worker agents. It split into security against malicious peers, tracing which agent caused a failure, and latent agent-to-agent channels that LatentLens and Chasm found unhelpful or exploitable.
editorial.whats_new: Hugging Face (Nov 26) published reproducible recipes for training multi-agent teams, the first about $50 on two H200s, a day after MeterRouter matched the strongest multi-agent system's accuracy at 82% lower cost on five benchmarks.
editorial.why_it_matters: The thread has moved from what fails in agent teams to what they cost: per-query routing under a dollar budget and cheap team training make cost a tunable you can benchmark, not a fixed overhead of going multi-agent.
editorial.take_for_builders: Record per-query token cost next to accuracy in your multi-agent evals, and keep KV-cache or latent hand-offs between models behind the same injection guards as text messages until Chasm-style defenses ship.

storylines.label: Inkling Mini
storylines.latest_title: Show HN: Rust agent with an Inkling 2 Mini inference engine for Apple Silicon

editorial.tldr: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on Nov 20: a looped multimodal MoE with about 26B total parameters, roughly 3B active per token, and a 1M-token context. vLLM shipped day-0 serving on Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark the same day, with a Docker image.
editorial.whats_new: Five days after launch, an agent-driven tuning run pushed single-user decode on one RTX PRO 6000 from 136 to 190.6 tok/s, and a Rust engine now serves the model on Apple silicon behind an OpenAI-compatible API.
editorial.why_it_matters: A 26B MoE with about 3B active parameters and 1M context now has serving paths on datacenter GPUs, one workstation card and Macs, so local coding-agent backends no longer need a hosted API.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you run a local coding-agent backend, benchmark Inkling 2 Mini with the vLLM Docker image on your own hardware before adopting the community tuning numbers.

status.detail: Open-weight release with vLLM support at launch; community tuning and non-CUDA runtimes followed within a week.

storylines.label: Visual Multimodal
storylines.latest_title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study

editorial.tldr: This is a research-theme thread, not one event: 22 items, mostly arXiv preprints, from Nov 9 to Nov 25 on visual agents, multimodal benchmarks and hallucination fixes. Mid-month the work shifted from new benchmarks (WebArena-Pro, MM-ReportBench, Google's Multimodal Knowledge Agent Benchmark) to agents that fetch visual evidence with tools.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 25 study found that adding a generated helper image to visual QA lowered mean accuracy by 3.7 points across 13 model pairs, while EVA the same day cut hallucinations by checking answers against tool-gathered visual evidence.
editorial.why_it_matters: For multimodal agents, the reliable gains in this thread come from grounding answers in fetched or re-read visual evidence; generating extra images or always sending pixels adds cost without a proven accuracy gain.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before adding image generation or always-on image inputs to a multimodal agent, run an ablation on your own eval set; prefer zoom, crop and re-check tools that tie each answer to visual evidence.

status.detail: Preprints only, no shipped products: evidence-seeking visual agents are the common direction, and one negative result questions image generation as a reasoning aid.

storylines.label: Empirical Study
storylines.latest_title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study

editorial.tldr: This is not one story: the seven papers share only the phrase "case study" or "empirical study" in their titles. They form a loose November run of arXiv work that measures how agents and models actually behave, covering where long-horizon errors enter, what token spend tracks, KV cache reuse, benchmark throttling, web-element hallucination and over-editing coding agents.
editorial.whats_new: The newest paper finds that adding a generated helper image to visual question answering lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 points across 13 model pairs, with declines on nine of ten tasks.
editorial.why_it_matters: The common thread is measurement: several of these papers test whether a number teams already rely on (pass rate, token spend, benchmark score) means what they assume it means.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you gate coding-agent patches on passing tests alone, add a diff-size or revert-and-retest check, because a passing patch can still carry edits the tests never needed.

storylines.label: Question Answering
storylines.latest_title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering

editorial.tldr: This is a research-theme thread of unrelated arXiv QA papers, not a single event. It opened Nov 12 with SAGE-QA questioning Exact Match scoring on SQuAD 2.0, then JET (Nov 17) targeted tool-calling agents that keep exploring a repository after they already have enough to answer.
editorial.whats_new: Two Nov 25 papers turn to QA memory: scene-graph memory repairs lift answerability from 27.2% to 37.4% without reliably improving QA accuracy, and Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent gains on generated questions but is mixed on human ones.
editorial.why_it_matters: Across all four papers, the proxy metric (Exact Match, answerability, generated-question scores) diverges from real answer quality, so RAG and agent evals built on those proxies can misreport progress.
editorial.take_for_builders: Before trusting a QA or RAG eval gain, check it against a hand-graded sample of real user questions; treat all four papers as preprints until reproduced.

storylines.label: Large Language
storylines.latest_title: VulnSafe: Measuring Vulnerability-Aware Relational Safety in Large Language Models

editorial.tldr: This slug used to track speculative decoding; after reclustering it holds 35 unrelated arXiv papers from Nov 9 onward whose only link is "Large Language Models" in the title. Read it as a research digest: most papers question how LLMs are evaluated, measure hallucination and uncertainty, or probe safety, with a few on infra such as LM-SimBench and MemOnce.
editorial.whats_new: Two more benchmarks landed Nov 25: Merlin-Bench finds 10 frontier LLMs struggle to produce proofs a formal verifier accepts, and VulnSafe scores eight models on 2,050 Chinese relational-safety prompts.
editorial.why_it_matters: There is no single event here. The useful signal is that eval methodology itself keeps getting challenged (shifting human raters, adaptive users, unvalidated user simulators), which is the layer your agent eval harness depends on.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent evals rely on a user simulator or LLM-as-judge, validate it against a small human-labeled set before trusting a week-over-week regression signal.

storylines.label: Speculative Decoding
storylines.latest_title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity

editorial.tldr: This is a research-theme thread, not one event: three weeks of independent arXiv papers on speculative decoding, from separate groups. Early work retargeted drafter training at acceptance length (D-REAL, REAL Loss), then the focus moved to block-diffusion draft trees and serving-side wins like grammar-forced drafts and KV reuse.
editorial.whats_new: DFly2 (Nov 25) drops the drafter's own KV cache and reuses the target's cache and sparse-attention selections, reporting more accepted tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark on long contexts.
editorial.why_it_matters: Speculative decoding is a near-free throughput lever in vLLM-class stacks, and these papers show the gains now hinge on drafter training, tree shape, and cache sharing rather than drafter size.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you serve structured or tool-call outputs, benchmark grammar-forced drafting and draft temperature calibration on your own traffic before swapping drafter architectures; treat paper speedups as unreplicated.

storylines.label: Activation Steering
storylines.latest_title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination

editorial.tldr: A Nov 13 paper argued that SAE steering applied to every token pushes representations off-distribution and proposed per-token gating that follows the generation trajectory. A Nov 19 paper then recast RL post-training of diffusion transformers as activation steering, tying a costly training step to an inference-time intervention.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 25 paper, TASK memory, pairs each text memory note with activation steering and a removable knowledge edit, reporting memory-ignoring errors cut to at most 1.5% across ten model-dataset cells on frozen LLMs.
editorial.why_it_matters: Activation steering is moving from a behavior knob into agent memory, so teams fighting memory hallucination on open-weight models get a no-fine-tuning option beyond better retrieval and prompting.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent ignores or misuses its stored notes on a frozen open-weight model, add a memory-ignoring error rate to your evals now so you can compare TASK-style steering against your current retrieval setup.

storylines.label: On-Policy Distillation
storylines.latest_title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents

editorial.tldr: On Nov 8 an arXiv paper measured how much quantized or asynchronous rollout mismatch on-policy distillation (OPD) tolerates. Over Nov 9-10, three papers pushed OPD into agent training: recovering skills lost to best-checkpoint GRPO selection, picking teacher reference trajectories for multi-turn tool use, and training coding-agent file-memory habits.
editorial.whats_new: Nov 25: CARE-OPD, an arXiv paper, replays trajectory prefixes during on-policy distillation of long-horizon agents and reports 59.5% on SWE-bench Verified with 45% less training time than asynchronous online OPD.
editorial.why_it_matters: OPD is becoming a standard agent post-training step, and rollout generation is its dominant cost; CARE-OPD and the mismatch study both target that cost directly.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you distill long-horizon or coding agents on-policy, benchmark prefix replay against your async online OPD before buying more rollout compute; CARE-OPD's 45% saving is self-reported and unreplicated.

status.detail: A cluster of arXiv papers adapting OPD to agents and cutting its rollout cost; no independent replication yet.
